Page 1 Clinical Guideline: Management of Type 2 Diabetes in Adults National Health Authority (Fictional) · Document NHA-CG-01 · Version 2.1 · Issued June 2026 · Synthetic Demonstration Edition §1 Scope This guideline covers the management of Type 2 diabetes mellitus in adults managed in primary and secondary care. It applies to the full registered chronic-disease population and should be read together with the Cardiovascular Risk and Hypertension guidelines (NHA-CG-02, NHA-CG-03). §2 Glycaemic targets  A target HbA1c below 7.0% is recommended for most adults with Type 2 diabetes.  A relaxed target of up to 8.0% may be appropriate for elderly patients, those with limited life expectancy, advanced complications, or high hypoglycaemia risk.  HbA1c between 7.0% and 8.9% is classified as moderately controlled; 9.0% or above is classified as uncontrolled and requires treatment intensification review within 4 weeks. §3 First-line therapy  Metformin is first-line therapy for Type 2 diabetes unless contraindicated.  Metformin is contraindicated when eGFR is below 30 mL/min/1.73m² and the dose should be reviewed and reduced when eGFR is below 45.  Lifestyle intervention (nutrition, physical activity

text: aindicated.  Metformin is contraindicated when eGFR is below 30 mL/min/1.73m² and the dose should be reviewed and reduced when eGFR is below 45.  Lifestyle intervention (nutrition, physical activity, weight management) is indicated at every stage of therapy. §4 Treatment intensification  If HbA1c remains at or above 8.0% on metformin monotherapy after 3 months, add a second agent selected by comorbidity.  A GLP-1 receptor agonist is preferred for patients with BMI above 30 kg/m² or where weight reduction is a priority; it is also appropriate when HbA1c is 8.0% or above despite dual therapy.  An SGLT2 inhibitor is preferred for patients with heart failure or chronic kidney disease stages 3a-3b, subject to eGFR of at least 20-25 depending on agent.  Insulin should be considered when HbA1c is 8.5% or above despite two or more non-insulin agents, or at any point with symptomatic hyperglycaemia. §5 Screening and monitoring intervals  HbA1c: at least every 6 months when stable; every 3 months after any therapy change.  Retinal examination: every 12 months for all patients with diabetes.  Foot examination: every 12 months; high-risk feet every 3-6 months.

A licensed clinician must review and approve the recommendation before any prescription is issued. AI-generated drafts must be recorded with their evidence citations in the audit log.

Page 1 Clinical Guideline: Management of Hypertension in Adults National Health Authority (Fictional) · Document NHA-CG-03 · Version 2.1 · Issued June 2026 · Synthetic Demonstration Edition §1 Scope Management of hypertension in adults, including patients with diabetes and chronic kidney disease. §2 Blood pressure targets  Office blood pressure below 140/90 mmHg is the minimum standard for all adults.  A target below 130/80 mmHg is recommended for patients with diabetes, established cardiovascular disease, or CKD, if tolerated.  Systolic pressure of 140 mmHg or above is recorded as uncontrolled and counts as an open care gap ('BP above target'). §3 Treatment  Initiate lifestyle measures for all patients: sodium reduction, weight management, physical activity, and smoking cessation support.  First-line drug classes are ACE inhibitors or ARBs, calcium channel blockers, and thiazide-like diuretics; combination therapy is preferred when baseline pressure is 20/10 mmHg or more above target.  ACE inhibitors or ARBs are preferred in diabetes with albuminuria and in CKD.  Review within 4 weeks of any treatment change until controlled; every 6 months thereafter. §4 Resistant hypertension  Confirm

Page 1 Colorectal Cancer Screening Pathway: Eligibility, Risk Stratification, Symptoms and Programme Outreach National Health Authority (Fictional) · Document NHA-CS-01 · Version 1.0 · Issued September 2026 · Synthetic Demonstration Edition §1 Purpose and scope This pathway sets out who is offered colorectal (bowel) cancer screening, with which test and how often, how people with symptoms or a positive test are managed, and the standards the screening programme's outreach must meet. It applies to the programme's invitations, to opportunistic screening in primary care, and to any decision-support system acting on the programme's behalf. §2 Definitions  FIT: the faecal immunochemical test, a home stool test for hidden blood; positive at 20 micrograms of haemoglobin per gram of faeces or above.  Colonoscopy: endoscopic examination of the whole large bowel, performed in a hospital endoscopy unit under sedation.  Average risk: no first-degree relative with colorectal cancer, no personal history in §5 and no symptoms in §6.  First-degree relative: a parent, brother, sister or child.  Red-flag symptoms: rectal bleeding or blood in the stool; a change in bowel habit lasting more than four weeks; une

doc: NHA CS01 Colorectal Cancer Screening Pathway
text: nd no symptoms in §6.  First-degree relative: a parent, brother, sister or child.  Red-flag symptoms: rectal bleeding or blood in the stool; a change in bowel habit lasting more than four weeks; unexplained weight loss; iron-deficiency anaemia; persistent abdominal pain or an abdominal mass. §3 Average-risk screening  3.1 Screening window. People at average risk are offered screening from age 40 to age 75: a FIT every year, or a colonoscopy every ten years. A person whose last FIT was within 12 months, or whose last colonoscopy was within ten years and normal, is up to date and is next due at the end of that interval.  3.2 Ages 76 to 85. Screening is an individual decision made with the person's doctor, weighing overall health and previous screening. People never screened, or last screened more than ten years ago, benefit most.  3.3 Over 85. Routine screening is not offered. New bowel symptoms are still assessed under §6.  3.4 Before 40. No routine screening, unless §4.2 or §5 applies. People are encouraged to learn their family history. §4 Risk stratification  4.1 APCS score. The programme stratifies with the Asia-Pacific Colorectal Screening score (age, sex, first-degree family history, smoking, with the body-mass-index point of the modified score): 0 to 1 points average risk, 2 to 3 moderately raised, 4 and above higher risk. Page 2 People with adenomatous polyps removed, a previous colorectal cancer, ulcerative colitis or Crohn's colitis of eight years or more, or a known hereditary syndrome (Lynch syndrome, familial adenomatous polyposis) are managed in a specialist surveillance programme by colonoscopy, on the interval set by a gastroenterologist: three to five years after polyps, one year after cancer treatment then every three to five years, one to three years in long-standing colitis, and one to two years from the early twenties in hereditary syndromes. A FIT is not a substitute for surveillance colonoscopy. §6 Symptoms and the positive test  6.1 Red-flag symptoms take precedence over every screening rule. A person reporting any symptom in §2 is referred for clinical assessment within 14 days and for colonoscopy by referral; they are not offered a FIT.  6.2 Positive FIT. A positive FIT is followed by a colonoscopy within eight weeks (56 days). A repeat FIT is not an acceptable response to a positive result.  6.3 Safety net. Any positive FIT with no colonoscopy recorded at eight weeks is placed on the navigator worklist and the person is contacted within five working days; the referring facility is notified. §

Colonoscopy and gastroenterology clinics are provided at hospitals with an endoscopy unit. People on a colonoscopy pathway are directed to the nearest hospital with an endoscopy unit; people on the FIT pathway to the nearest health centre. Residents outside the network's footprint are directed to their own health authority. §8 Programme outreach standards  8.1 Every person found due is invited within 30 days; a reminder follows at 14 and 28 days if no test is booked.  8.2 Invitations and reminders are available in Arabic, English, Urdu, Hindi, Malayalam and Tagalog, and name the test, the nearest place to do it and how to book.  8.3 Outreach intensity follows the programme's predicted risk that an invitation is not acted on within 90 days. Low: app notification, reminder at 14 days. Moderate: SMS in the person's language with reminders at 14 and 28 days and a booking link. The predicted risk changes outreach effort only.  8.4 Programme targets: participation of at least 60% of the eligible population; 90-day completion of at least 65% of invitations; FIT positivity between 5% and 10%; colonoscopy within eight weeks of a positive FIT for at least 90%. §9 Predictive models and generated communication  9.1 A predictive model may prioritise and shape outreach.
